newsitem.title: USA: Stay in Hong Kong, eye China - business executives.
newsitem.headline: Stay in Hong Kong, eye China - business executives.

text.p: A group of international business executives gave ringing endorsements of Hong Kong as the best vantage point to take part in the huge China market.

In a conference on Hong Kong's business future on Wednesday, several prominent international business leaders expressed their confidence in Hong Kong's future as a financial hub for the region and a springboard to China.
David Eldon, chief executive officer of Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp, saw Hong Kong playing a vital role within China both as its international financial center and its capital formation base.
The major proportion of China's H share trading takes place in Hong Kong.
"The development of a debt market and of financial futures for China will be the next stage," he said.
The eventual convertibility of the renminbi will present even greater possibilities for the Hong Kong markets, Eldon said.
Half of China's trade with the world and a third of its foreign exchange earnings flow through Hong Kong, said James Hulihan, group executive vice president of Bank of America.
"The real attraction of being in Hong Kong is ... what our friends in the real estate business call -- location, location and location," he said.
Hong Kong's role as a gateway to the vast China market is underscored by Patrick Siewert, vice president of Eastman Kodak Co.
From a base of 150 retail sites in Hong Kong, Kodak opened 2,000 express photo-processing locations in some 200 Chinese cities in the past two years, he said.
"Hong Kong continues to play a very important 'standard setting' role in this expansion effort," he said.
Trevor Rowe, chairman for the Asia Pacific Region at Salomon Brothers Inc, praised Hong Kong's "skills in cross-border logistics" that are invaluable for international companies operating in Asia.

After reversion to Chinese sovereignty, Hong Kong is likely to become a "more chaotic and more vibrant Singapore" where business can thrive in creative tension free of centrally directed economic planning, he said.
But several executives also expressed their concerns about Hong Kong's competitiveness.

"We are concerned about the fact that costs are rising and that it is not often easy to get the right kind of staff," said Bank of America's Hulihan. "The environment, as in most major Asian cities, is increasingly a problem."
